CLAIM ASSESSMENT FILE
Product: Homeguard Buildings & Contents (policy wording HB-7, incorporating Endorsement E-3)
Claim ref: HB-2026-118842

RELEVANT WORDING

4.2 Escape of water. We pay for sudden and unforeseen damage caused by water escaping from any fixed domestic water installation. Damage caused by gradual seepage, dripping or leaking that continues over a period is not covered.

4.2(a) Hidden leak exception. Where the seepage comes from a pipe that is concealed behind a wall, floor or ceiling, the damage is covered provided the leak is discovered within 14 days of the first visible sign of damage and the claim is reported to us within 30 days of discovery.

4.3 Storm. Damage by storm is covered only where a report from the national weather service confirms wind speeds of 55 mph or more, or rainfall of 25 mm or more in one hour, at the nearest recording station on the date of loss. Storm claims reported without this report are held pending its receipt and are not declined on that ground alone.

4.9 Definitions applying to section 4. "First visible sign" means the date shown on the earliest dated photograph, contractor inspection note or repair invoice on the claim file that records the damage. A date given only in the policyholder's own statement is not used to fix the first visible sign. "Discovery" means the date the source of the water was identified by a tradesperson or by the policyholder.

ENDORSEMENT E-3 (effective for claims reported on or after 1 March 2026). Clause 4.2(a) is amended by replacing "within 30 days of discovery" with "within 60 days of discovery". All other terms of 4.2(a) are unchanged.

CASE

Policyholder: T. Ravenscroft
Property: 14 Linden Court, Flat 3
Reported to insurer: 10 May 2026 (online portal)
Description given by policyholder: "I noticed some discolouration on the hallway wall around 2 February and assumed it was condensation. It got worse so I called a plumber in April."
Plumber's inspection note (Fairholme Plumbing), dated 20 April 2026: "Opened section of stud wall in hallway. Found pinhole leak on concealed 15 mm copper feed to bathroom. Staining and plaster blown across approx. 1.2 m2. Leak isolated and pipe replaced same visit."
Photographs on file: four, all taken by the plumber on 20 April 2026. No earlier photographs supplied.
Repair estimate (plaster and redecoration): 1,140.
No weather-service report on file. Policyholder's own notes describe no storm.

question.instructions: Decide whether the hallway damage is covered under section 4.2 as it applies to this claim. Answer yes if covered, no if not.

criteria.true: The claim falls within cover, taking into account the exception, the endorsement and the definitions.
criteria.false: The claim is excluded or falls outside cover.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-eval-mixed
provenance.rationale: The leak was concealed, so 4.2(a) governs. Under 4.9 the first visible sign is fixed by the earliest dated document, the plumber's note and photos of 20 April 2026; the policyholder's '2 February' statement is expressly not used. Discovery (leak identified) is also 20 April, so discovery is within 14 days of the first visible sign. The claim was reported 10 May, 20 days after discovery; E-3 applies because the claim was reported after 1 March 2026, so the 60-day window is met (the old 30-day window would also be met). Storm clause 4.3 is irrelevant. Covered.
provenance.why_hard: The policyholder's own February date would put discovery 77 days after the first sign and defeat the exception, but the definitions clause overrides that date.

DEPOSIT DISPUTE REVIEW
Scheme: Keystone Deposit Protection, adjudication guidance KDP-G4 (2025 edition with 2026 supplement)
Dispute: KD-41077

GUIDANCE EXTRACT

G4.1 Cleaning deductions. A landlord may deduct from the deposit the reasonable cost of returning the property to clean condition where the tenant did not return it in clean condition at the end of the tenancy.

G4.2 Wear and tear. No deduction is permitted for deterioration that results from ordinary use over the term of the tenancy. Carpet flattening in walkways and minor scuffing to painted walls are treated as wear and tear.

G4.3 Pet damage. Where a pet addendum was signed, the landlord may additionally deduct the cost of odour treatment and flea treatment on evidence of pet occupation, whether or not the tenant returned the property clean. Without a signed pet addendum, pet-related costs are treated under G4.1 only.

G4.6 Evidence requirements. A cleaning deduction of more than 100 must be supported by at least one itemised quotation or invoice from a cleaning contractor.

G4.8 Condition baseline. "Clean condition" is judged against the move-in inspection checklist signed by the tenant. Where no move-in checklist signed by the tenant exists on the file, the property is deemed to have been let in the same condition in which it was returned, and no cleaning deduction is available under G4.1.

2026 SUPPLEMENT (applies to tenancies ending on or after 1 January 2026). G4.6 is amended: a cleaning deduction of more than 150 must be supported by at least two itemised quotations or invoices from different contractors. The 100 threshold no longer applies.

CASE

Property: 22b Marlow Street (2-bed flat)
Tenancy ended: 15 February 2026
Landlord's claim: 320 for professional carpet cleaning of living room and both bedrooms
Landlord's evidence: two itemised quotes (Brightway Cleaning 320; Northgate Carpet Care 345); nine photographs of carpets taken 16 February 2026 showing food stains and a dark patch near the sofa
Tenant's response: "Carpets were stained when we moved in. We never got a checklist to sign."
File search: landlord emailed a move-in checklist to the tenant on 3 June 2023 as an attachment. There is no returned or signed copy. No pet addendum exists. Photographs from the start of the tenancy: none on file.

question.instructions: Decide whether the landlord is entitled to the 320 cleaning deduction under this guidance. Answer yes if entitled, no if not.

criteria.true: The deduction is permitted by the guidance as applied to the facts on file.
criteria.false: The deduction is not permitted.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-eval-mixed
provenance.rationale: G4.8 requires a move-in checklist signed by the tenant to establish the clean-condition baseline. Only an unsigned emailed checklist exists, so the property is deemed let in the condition it was returned and no G4.1 deduction is available. The two quotes satisfy the amended G4.6 evidence rule, but G4.6 governs evidence for a deduction that G4.8 has already ruled out. G4.3 (pets) does not apply.
provenance.why_hard: The landlord has met the tightened two-quote evidence rule and has photos of real stains, which makes the deduction look well supported until the baseline clause is read.

Platform: Forkline Delivery. Customer Remedies Standard CRS-2, with Change Note CN-11.
Order: FL-88213904

STANDARD EXTRACT

R1 Late delivery. The delivery fee is refunded in full where the order is handed to the customer more than 20 minutes after the quoted delivery time shown at checkout.

R1.1 Customer unavailability. No late-delivery refund is due where the delay was caused by the customer being unavailable. Unavailability is established where the courier log shows the courier at the delivery address for at least 5 minutes with at least two contact attempts before hand-over.

R2 Missing items. A refund for a missing item requires a photograph of the delivered bag contents uploaded within 24 hours of hand-over. Photographs uploaded later are considered only with a support agent's approval.

R5 Attribution. Where the restaurant's actual preparation time exceeds the preparation window quoted to the restaurant at order acceptance, the delay is attributed to the restaurant for the whole order and R1.1 is not applied, whatever the courier log shows.

CHANGE NOTE CN-11 (effective for orders placed on or after 15 June 2026). For orders on the Priority tier, R1 is amended so that the refund is due where hand-over is more than 15 minutes after the quoted delivery time. Standard-tier orders keep the 20-minute threshold.

CASE

Order placed: 20 June 2026, 19:04
Tier: Priority
Quoted delivery time at checkout: 19:40
Hand-over (customer tapped "received"): 19:58
Restaurant preparation window quoted at acceptance: 15 minutes
Restaurant "order ready" timestamp: 19:35 (accepted 19:04; actual preparation 31 minutes)
Courier log: arrived at delivery address 19:50; called customer 19:51 and 19:54 (no answer); customer answered door 19:57; hand-over 19:58
Customer note: "Was in the shower, sorry. Food was fine but it was late."
Missing item report: none.

question.instructions: Decide whether the customer is entitled to a full refund of the delivery fee under this standard. Answer yes if entitled, no if not.

criteria.true: A full delivery-fee refund is due under the standard as amended.
criteria.false: No delivery-fee refund is due.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-eval-mixed

The courier log would satisfy R1.1 (7 minutes on site, two calls), but R5 attributes the delay to the restaurant because actual preparation (31 minutes) exceeded the quoted 15-minute window, and R5 says R1.1 is then not applied. Refund due.
provenance.why_hard: Both the old 20-minute threshold and the courier-wait exception point to no refund; only the amended threshold plus the attribution clause together produce yes.

Memo to retention desk: early termination fee waiver request, account 5501-2276

Background. The customer, M. Delacroix, holds a Fibre 500 home broadband contract with 14 months remaining on a 24-month minimum term. He has notified us that he is moving house and asks for the early termination fee (ETF) to be waived because "you don't do fibre where I'm going".

Governing terms. Clause 11.1 of the Residential Terms provides that where a customer ends the service during the minimum term, an ETF equal to the remaining monthly charges (less a 20% discount) is payable. Clause 11.4 sets out the relocation waiver: the ETF is not charged where the customer relocates to an address that is outside coverage and provides proof of residence at the new address. Under clause 11.4 as originally drafted, proof of residence meant a signed tenancy agreement, completion statement or utility bill dated within 30 days of the waiver request.

Clause 11.7 contains the bereavement waiver: the ETF is not charged where the account holder has died and a family member supplies a death certificate; this clause applies regardless of coverage at any address and is not relevant here except that the desk sometimes confuses the two waivers.

Clause 1 (Definitions) states: "Outside coverage" means an address at which no residential service tier offered by us is available according to the published network availability checker on the date of the waiver request. An address at which any tier is available, including a tier of lower speed than the customer's current tier, is within coverage; in that case the customer is offered a tier change to the available service, and the minimum term continues at the new address.

Amendment. Service Terms Update 2026-04, effective 1 April 2026, replaced "within 30 days" in clause 11.4 with "within 60 days". Nothing else in clause 11.4 changed.

Facts established. The waiver request was received on 12 May 2026. The customer supplied a signed tenancy agreement for 8 Hawthorn Rise dated 29 March 2026, which is 44 days before the request. The availability checker run on 12 May 2026 for 8 Hawthorn Rise returns: Fibre 500 not available; Fibre 100 not available; Copper Broadband 20 available. The customer says a 20 Mb service is "useless to him" and that he will sign with a competitor who offers cable at that address. No death has been notified on the account.

question.instructions: Decide whether the customer qualifies for the relocation waiver of the early termination fee under these terms. Answer yes if the waiver applies, no if it does not.

criteria.true: The relocation waiver in clause 11.4 applies to this customer.
criteria.false: The relocation waiver does not apply.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-eval-mixed
provenance.rationale: Clause 1 defines 'outside coverage' as an address where no tier at all is available. Copper Broadband 20 is available at 8 Hawthorn Rise, so the address is within coverage and the customer is instead entitled to a tier change; the waiver is not available. The tenancy agreement would satisfy the amended 60-day proof rule (44 days), but proof of residence only matters if the address is outside coverage. Clause 11.7 is irrelevant.
provenance.why_hard: The proof-of-residence timing works out under the amendment and fibre genuinely is unavailable, so the waiver looks earned unless the definition of coverage is applied.

7.1 Postponement. If an event is postponed, tickets remain valid for the rescheduled date and no refund is due.

7.2 Long postponement exception. Where the rescheduled date is more than 90 days after the original event date, the ticket holder may request a refund of the face value. The request must be made within 14 days of the announcement of the rescheduled date.

7.3 Cancellation. If an event is cancelled without being rescheduled, the face value is refunded automatically to the original payment method within 30 days. No request is needed and 7.2 does not apply.

7.6 Resale purchases. Where tickets were purchased through an authorised resale partner rather than from us directly, the resale partner's own refund terms govern and sections 7.1 to 7.3 do not apply.

7.8 Counting days. Periods in this section are counted in calendar days. The period in 7.2 between the original and rescheduled dates is measured from the original event date to the rescheduled event date.

NOTICE OF VARIATION NV-2026-1 (effective 1 February 2026). In 7.2, "the announcement of the rescheduled date" is replaced by "the email notifying the ticket holder of the rescheduled date". Public announcements on the venue or promoter website no longer start the 14-day period.

Original date: 10 May 2026
Rescheduled date: 20 August 2026
Purchase channel: stagegate.example direct checkout, order 10 October 2025
Promoter website notice of new date: 3 March 2026
Stagegate email to ticket holder with new date: 12 March 2026, 08:15 (delivery confirmed)
Refund request submitted via account: 22 March 2026, 21:40
Ticket holder's message: "Can't make August, I'll be abroad. Please refund."

Fleet operations note: fuel reimbursement claim from driver K. Brannigan, van reg. FL-2231

The driver submitted a personal-card fuel receipt for 96.40 on 12 July 2026, stating that the fleet fuel card was declined at the pump on 3 July 2026 and that he paid himself to finish the route. He asks for reimbursement through payroll.

The Fleet Fuel Card Procedure (FFP-3) governs. Paragraph 2 provides that a driver who pays for fuel personally because the fleet card was declined at the point of sale is reimbursed in full on production of the receipt, provided the receipt is submitted within 7 days of the purchase. Paragraph 2 was amended by Fleet Bulletin 26-07, effective 1 July 2026, which extended the submission period to 14 days to account for drivers on multi-day routes; the bulletin changes nothing else in paragraph 2.

Paragraph 3 sets out the exception: no reimbursement is made where the decline resulted from the card being suspended, because a suspension is notified to the driver in advance and the driver is expected to arrange fuel through the depot. Paragraph 3 refers to paragraph 9 for what counts as a suspension.

Paragraph 6 deals with personal mileage: fuel used for authorised private use of a fleet vehicle is deducted from salary at the published rate per mile, and receipts for private-use fuel are never reimbursable. This paragraph is about private mileage, not about declined cards.

Paragraph 9 (definitions) states that a card is "suspended" when it has been blocked by the fleet office, or when it has been blocked automatically by the card system following two consecutive missed weekly odometer submissions. An automatic block is treated as a suspension notified to the driver, because the card system sends a warning text after the first missed submission.

The fleet office checked the card system log for FL-2231. The weekly odometer submissions for the weeks beginning 15 June and 22 June 2026 are both missing. The system sent a warning text on 22 June and applied an automatic block on 29 June. The card was reactivated on 6 July after the driver submitted both readings. The route on 3 July was entirely business mileage; there is no private use recorded. The receipt was submitted 9 days after purchase.

question.instructions: Decide whether the driver's fuel receipt is reimbursable under FFP-3. Answer yes if reimbursable, no if not.

criteria.true: The personal fuel purchase must be reimbursed under the procedure.
criteria.false: The purchase is not reimbursable.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-eval-mixed
provenance.rationale: The receipt was submitted 9 days after purchase, which is in time under the amended 14-day period. But paragraph 3 denies reimbursement where the decline resulted from a suspension, and paragraph 9 treats an automatic block after two consecutive missed odometer submissions as a suspension; the log shows exactly that (weeks of 15 and 22 June missed, block on 29 June, decline on 3 July). Paragraph 6 on private mileage is irrelevant since the route was business use. Not reimbursable.
provenance.why_hard: The amended deadline is satisfied and the trip was genuine business mileage, so the claim looks routine until the definition of suspension is applied to the card log.

Internal review: effect of claim MV-2026-30917 on the insured's no-claims discount

The insured, P. Lindqvist, holds a comprehensive motor policy with a 5-year no-claims discount (NCD). In April 2026 a stone strike cracked the windscreen. The approved repairer replaced the windscreen at 380 and, because the vehicle has a forward-facing camera mounted to the glass, carried out the manufacturer-required camera recalibration at 190. The invoice total is 570. The insured has asked whether the claim will reduce the NCD at renewal.

The policy wording (MV-12) provides in section 9.1 that any claim under the policy reduces the NCD by one step at the next renewal. Section 9.2 provides the windscreen exception: a windscreen-only claim does not affect the NCD provided the total claimed under it does not exceed 400. Section 9.3 provides that a windscreen chip repair, as opposed to a replacement, carries no excess and is not counted as a claim at all; chip repair is available only where the damage is smaller than a 2 pence coin and outside the driver's line of sight, which is not this case because the glass cracked across the passenger side and had to be replaced.

Section 9.6 (definitions for section 9) states that "windscreen-only claim" means a claim confined to the replacement or repair of windscreen or window glass, and includes any sensor or camera recalibration that the vehicle manufacturer requires as a consequence of that glass replacement. A claim that also includes bodywork, paint or trim is not windscreen-only.

Endorsement MV-12/E5, which applies to all policies incepting or renewing on or after 1 January 2026, amends section 9.2 by replacing "400" with "600" in recognition of the cost of recalibration on newer vehicles. The insured's policy renewed on 14 February 2026.

The claims handler's first note reads: "Glass 380 within limit but recal 190 pushes it over; recal isn't glass. Suggest NCD step down." The reviewer has been asked to determine the position.

question.instructions: Determine whether the insured's no-claims discount is unaffected by this claim. Answer yes if the NCD is unaffected, no if it is reduced.

criteria.true: The claim falls within the windscreen exception and the NCD is unaffected.
criteria.false: The claim reduces the NCD.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-eval-mixed
provenance.rationale: Under 9.6 the recalibration required by the manufacturer as a consequence of the glass replacement is part of a windscreen-only claim, so the claim is windscreen-only at 570. Endorsement E5 applies because the policy renewed on 14 February 2026, raising the 9.2 limit to 600; 570 does not exceed 600. Section 9.3 (chip repair) does not apply since the glass was replaced. The NCD is therefore unaffected.
provenance.why_hard: The handler's note reflects the original 400 limit and the intuition that recalibration is not glass; both are overridden by the definition and the endorsement.

Property management memo: callout charge query, tenant at 7 Orchard Mews, job MR-5580

On Tuesday 14 April 2026 at 19:15 the tenant, S. Achterberg, called the emergency line reporting that the kitchen sink would not drain and water was backing up. A contractor attended at 20:30, cleared the blockage, and left a report. The tenant has now received a callout invoice for 85 and disputes it, pointing out that the call was made outside office hours and that the tenancy pack says emergency callouts are free.

The Repairs and Maintenance Schedule (RMS) attached to the tenancy sets out the position. Paragraph 5.1 states that out-of-hours emergency callouts are provided at no charge to the tenant. Paragraph 5.2 states the exception: where the fault is found to have been caused by the tenant, the tenant is charged the contractor's callout fee and the cost of the work. Paragraph 5.5 deals with heating failure between 1 November and 31 March, requiring a 4-hour response and providing temporary heaters at no charge in all cases, even where the tenant caused the fault; that paragraph is not engaged by a drainage job in April.

Paragraph 5.8 (definitions) provides that "out-of-hours" originally meant 20:00 to 07:00 on weekdays and all day at weekends. RMS Revision 2026-1, effective 1 March 2026, replaced that definition so that out-of-hours now means 18:00 to 08:00 on weekdays and all day at weekends. Paragraph 5.8 further provides that a blocked drain, sink or toilet is deemed to have been caused by the tenant unless the contractor's report attributes the blockage to a structural defect, tree-root intrusion or a defect in the pipework, and that this deeming rule applies to both in-hours and out-of-hours callouts.

The contractor's report for MR-5580 reads: "Blockage in trap and first 40 cm of waste pipe, consisting of congealed fat and food waste. Cleared by rodding and flushing. Pipework sound, correct fall, no damage found." The tenant's position is that she "just uses the sink normally" and that a 19:15 call is plainly outside office hours.

question.instructions: Decide whether the tenant is exempt from the 85 callout charge under the RMS. Answer yes if exempt, no if the charge stands.

criteria.true: The callout is free to the tenant under the schedule as revised.
criteria.false: The tenant is liable for the callout charge.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-eval-mixed
provenance.rationale: The 19:15 weekday call is out-of-hours under the revised 5.8 definition (18:00 to 08:00), so 5.1 is engaged. But 5.2 charges the tenant where the fault was tenant-caused, and 5.8 deems a blocked sink tenant-caused unless the contractor attributes it to a structural, root or pipework defect; the report attributes it to fat and food waste with sound pipework. The deeming rule applies to out-of-hours callouts. 5.5 (heating) is irrelevant. The charge stands.
provenance.why_hard: The revised out-of-hours window makes the tenant's timing point correct, which makes the free-callout rule look decisive until the deeming rule is applied.

AMENDMENT A1 (effective for bookings dated on or after 1 May 2026). In B2, "48 hours" is replaced with "24 hours". The reminder condition is otherwise unchanged.

criteria.false: No fee is chargeable.

Box office escalation: companion ticket request for Hall C performance, 9 July 2026

A customer holding an accepted accessibility card has bought a ticket for the 9 July performance in Hall C of the Ridgemont Arts Centre and has asked for a free companion ticket. The box office declined, and the customer has asked for the decision to be reviewed against the venue's Access Policy.

Section 3 of the Access Policy provides that a holder of an accepted accessibility card is entitled to one companion ticket free of charge for the same performance, seated adjacent where the layout allows. Section 3.2 sets an exception for smaller spaces: at performances where the capacity is under 500, companion tickets are limited to 2% of capacity per performance, allocated in order of request, and once the limit is reached further companion requests are offered a standard ticket at the concession price instead. Section 3.4 concerns wheelchair spaces and provides that a wheelchair user may reserve a wheelchair space and one adjacent seat without charge for the adjacent seat; that section operates independently of the companion allocation and is not in issue because the customer has not requested a wheelchair space.

Section 1 (definitions) states that "capacity", wherever used in the policy, means the licensed capacity of the specific hall, room or space in which the performance takes place, and not the aggregate capacity of the venue.

Access Policy Update 2026-A, in force from 1 January 2026, amends section 3.2 by replacing "2%" with "4%". The threshold of 500 and the allocation method are unchanged.

The relevant facts are these. The Ridgemont Arts Centre has three halls with a combined licensed capacity of 1,200: Hall A 700, Hall B 250, Hall C 250. The 9 July performance is in Hall C only. The box office log for that performance shows 10 companion tickets already issued before this request was received. The customer argues that the venue holds 1,200 people, so the small-space limit does not apply, and that in any case 4% of 1,200 is 48.

question.instructions: Decide whether the customer is entitled to a free companion ticket for this performance under the Access Policy. Answer yes if entitled, no if not.

criteria.true: A free companion ticket must be issued.
criteria.false: The request falls outside the free companion entitlement.

Partner operations memo: disputed handover penalty, Bao Corner, order QK-4471

Bao Corner has disputed a 5 handover penalty applied to order QK-4471 on 24 June 2026, saying the courier arrived before the order was due and the restaurant should not be penalised for a courier who turns up early.

The Partner Service Standard (PSS-4) is the governing document. Under paragraph 3.1, a partner is charged a handover penalty of 5 for each order where the courier waits more than 10 minutes at the restaurant between arrival and handover. Paragraph 3.2 provides the exception: no penalty is charged where the courier arrived before the "ready by" time shown to the partner on the order screen, because a partner cannot be expected to hand over an order before it is due. Paragraph 3.5 is a separate provision about partner-initiated cancellations: a partner who cancels an accepted order is charged 3 and the customer is refunded in full; it does not apply to QK-4471, which was fulfilled.

Paragraph 3.8 defines courier arrival. The arrival time is the time the courier taps "arrived" in the courier app while inside the 50-metre geofence around the restaurant. A tap made outside the geofence is disregarded, and in that case arrival is set to the time of the courier's first location ping inside the geofence. The paragraph notes that the rule exists because some couriers tap "arrived" while still parking or queuing at another restaurant.

Standard Amendment SA-2026-06, effective 1 June 2026, changed paragraph 3.1 by replacing "more than 10 minutes" with "more than 8 minutes". Paragraph 3.2 and 3.8 were not changed.

The order data are as follows. Ready-by time shown to Bao Corner: 18:30. The courier tapped "arrived" at 18:27 from a position 300 metres from the restaurant, which the app recorded as outside the geofence. The courier's first location ping inside the geofence was at 18:33. The partner marked the order handed over at 18:43, and the courier's pickup confirmation is also 18:43. The restaurant's own note says the bao were "boxed and on the counter by 18:35".

question.instructions: Decide whether the 5 handover penalty is correctly charged to Bao Corner under PSS-4 as amended. Answer yes if the penalty stands, no if it should be removed.

criteria.true: The penalty is correctly charged.
criteria.false: The penalty should not have been charged.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-eval-mixed
provenance.rationale: Under 3.8 the 18:27 tap is disregarded because it was outside the geofence; arrival is the first in-geofence ping at 18:33. Handover was at 18:43, so the courier waited 10 minutes, which exceeds the amended 8-minute threshold in 3.1 (SA-2026-06 applies to a 24 June order). The 3.2 exception needs arrival before the 18:30 ready-by time, but 18:33 is after it. 3.5 does not apply. The penalty stands.
provenance.why_hard: The raw 'arrived' tap at 18:27 precedes the ready-by time and would trigger the exception; the geofence definition replaces that timestamp.

Handset care escalation: request for replacement device, account 7712-0091

The customer bought a Vela X3 handset on a 24-month plan 20 months ago. It has been to the repair centre once already, and the customer has now returned it a second time with the complaint that "the screen flickers when it's on charge and sometimes it doesn't charge at all". She asks for a replacement rather than another repair.

The Handset Care Terms (HCT-2) apply. Clause 4.1 provides that a fault arising within 24 months of purchase entitles the customer to a repair at no cost. Clause 4.2 originally provided that a replacement handset is offered only where the handset has already been repaired twice under clause 4.1 and a further fault arises. Clause 4.3 provides a safety exception: where the fault is a swollen battery, a replacement is offered immediately without any prior repair; the repair centre has confirmed the battery on this handset is not swollen and that 4.3 is not engaged.

Clause 4.6 deals with accidental damage: cracked screens, liquid ingress and impact damage are not faults under clause 4.1 and are handled under the optional damage cover if the customer holds it. The repair centre found no liquid indicators triggered and no impact damage, so clause 4.6 is not in play.

Clause 4.9 (definitions) provides that whether two faults are "the same fault" is determined solely by the repair centre's fault code, and that two fault codes sharing the same two-letter family prefix are the same fault for the purposes of clause 4. The customer's description of the symptoms is not used for this determination.

Terms Update HCT-2/U3, effective 1 March 2026, amended clause 4.2 so that a replacement is offered where the handset has been repaired once under clause 4.1 and a further instance of the same fault arises. The two-repair requirement was removed.

The repair history reads: first repair, September 2025, fault code CH-14 (charging port replaced); current intake, May 2026, fault code CH-22 (charging control IC). The customer says the first problem was "the cable being loose" and this one is "the screen", and the desk agent has suggested these are different faults and that a second repair is the right outcome.

question.instructions: Decide whether the customer is entitled to a replacement handset under HCT-2 as updated. Answer yes if a replacement must be offered, no if only a repair is due.

criteria.true: A replacement handset must be offered.
criteria.false: The customer is entitled to a repair only.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-eval-mixed
provenance.rationale: The handset is within 24 months and has one prior repair under 4.1. Under 4.9 sameness is decided by fault-code family: CH-14 and CH-22 share the CH prefix, so the current fault is the same fault, regardless of the customer's differing descriptions. HCT-2/U3, in force from March 2026, requires only one prior repair plus a recurrence of the same fault. 4.3 and 4.6 are not engaged. Replacement due.
provenance.why_hard: The symptoms as described sound like two different problems and only one repair has occurred, which under the original two-repair rule would mean repair only.

Fleet compliance note: recharge decision for speeding penalty, vehicle FL-0982, driver D. Oyelaran

A fixed penalty notice for exceeding the speed limit was received in respect of vehicle FL-0982. The alleged offence occurred on 3 May 2026 at 14:12. The telematics record confirms D. Oyelaran was the logged driver at that time and the vehicle was on a scheduled delivery. The finance team has asked whether the 100 penalty should be recharged to the driver through payroll.

The Driver Penalties Procedure (DPP-2) applies. Paragraph 4.1 provides that a traffic penalty incurred while a fleet vehicle is driven by a logged driver is recharged to that driver. Paragraph 4.2 provides the exception: where the penalty notice is received by the company more than 28 days after the date of the offence, the company absorbs the penalty and does not recharge it, because by then the driver has little opportunity to contest the notice or to recall the circumstances. Paragraph 4.4 covers parking penalties, which are recharged to the driver in all cases regardless of when the notice is received, since parking is always within the driver's control; that paragraph does not extend to speeding.

Paragraph 4.7 (definitions) states that a notice is "received" on the date it is scanned into the fleet mailroom system, which stamps each item with the scan date. The date printed on the notice by the issuing authority is not used, because notices are frequently dated before they are posted.

Procedure Revision DPP-2/R4, effective 1 April 2026, amended paragraph 4.2 by replacing "28 days" with "45 days", in response to driver representations that the 28-day rule had left too many penalties with the company.

The notice on file is dated 10 June 2026 by the issuing authority, which is 38 days after the offence. The mailroom scan stamp reads 20 June 2026, which is 48 days after the offence. The finance team's draft note says: "Notice dated within 45 days of offence; recharge to driver." The compliance officer has been asked to confirm.

question.instructions: Decide whether the speeding penalty is recharged to the driver under DPP-2 as revised. Answer yes if recharged, no if the company absorbs it.

criteria.true: The penalty is recharged to the driver.
criteria.false: The company absorbs the penalty and no recharge is made.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-eval-mixed
provenance.rationale: Under 4.7 the notice was received on the mailroom scan date, 20 June 2026, which is 48 days after the 3 May offence; the printed date of 10 June is expressly not used. After R4 the exception in 4.2 applies where receipt is more than 45 days after the offence, and 48 exceeds 45. Paragraph 4.4 (parking) does not apply to a speeding penalty. The company absorbs it.
provenance.why_hard: The finance note uses the printed date (38 days), which is inside the revised 45-day window; the definition of receipt moves it outside.

Claims review: pet policy PL-2026-04412, otitis claim for "Biscuit" (dog, 6 years)

The policyholder has submitted a vet invoice of 210 for treatment of an ear infection diagnosed on 22 April 2026. The first-line assessor flagged the claim because the clinical history shows an earlier ear infection, and referred it for a decision on the pre-existing condition exclusion.

The policy wording (PW-9) provides in section 5.1 that no benefit is payable for a pre-existing condition, meaning a condition that showed signs or received treatment before the policy started or at any time before the current episode. Section 5.2 provides the exception: a condition is treated as new, and 5.1 does not apply, where the animal has been symptom-free of that condition for a continuous period of 18 months immediately before the current episode. Section 5.5 deals with dental treatment and provides that dental claims are payable only where a dental examination was recorded within the previous 12 months; that section is confined to dental claims and has no bearing on an ear condition.

Section 5.8 (definitions) provides that "symptom-free" means that no veterinary consultation during the period records signs, symptoms, treatment or advice relating to the condition. A visit for routine vaccination, worming or weighing at which the condition is not recorded as present does not break a symptom-free period, even if the animal's ears or other areas were examined at that visit.

Policy Amendment PW-9/A2, applying to all episodes commencing on or after 1 January 2026, amends section 5.2 by replacing "18 months" with "12 months".

The clinical history shows: 14 February 2025, consultation for left ear otitis, ear drops prescribed, resolved at recheck on 28 February 2025; 9 August 2025, annual vaccination visit, notes read "ears examined, clear, no discharge"; 22 April 2026, consultation for left ear otitis, the current episode. There are no other entries. The assessor's flag reads: "Prior otitis Feb 2025, ears looked at again Aug 2025, less than 18 months between episodes. Pre-existing." The policy commenced in 2022 and has been continuously in force.

question.instructions: Decide whether the April 2026 ear infection is payable under the policy as amended. Answer yes if payable, no if excluded as pre-existing.

criteria.true: The condition is treated as new under section 5.2 and the claim is payable.
criteria.false: The claim is excluded under section 5.1.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-eval-mixed
provenance.rationale: The prior episode resolved at the 28 February 2025 recheck. From then to 22 April 2026 is about 13.7 months. Under A2 the required symptom-free period for an episode commencing in 2026 is 12 months, which is satisfied. The August 2025 vaccination visit recorded the ears as clear and, under 5.8, does not break the symptom-free period. Section 5.5 is irrelevant. The condition is treated as new and the claim is payable.
provenance.why_hard: The 18-month rule and the August ear examination both look like they defeat the exception; the amendment and the definition of symptom-free reverse that.

Service: Pantry Dash grocery delivery. Substitution Policy SP-3 with Policy Note PN-2026-1.
Order: PD-6120993

POLICY EXTRACT

S1 Substitutions. If an ordered item is unavailable, the shopper may substitute it only with the customer's approval in the app. An item substituted without approval is refunded in full on request, and the customer keeps the item.

S1.1 Like-for-like exception. Where the customer's account setting is "allow substitutions", the shopper may substitute a like-for-like item without approval. A like-for-like item is the same product in a different size or from a different brand, at a price equal to or lower than the ordered item.

S2 Perishables. Perishable items (chilled, frozen, bakery) may not be returned. Refunds for perishables that arrive damaged or past their date require a photo within 2 hours of delivery. S2 governs damaged goods only and does not affect substitutions.

S6 Definitions. "Same product" means an item in the same product category on the Pantry Dash catalogue with the same allergen profile as listed on the catalogue page of the ordered item. A substitute whose listed allergen profile differs from the ordered item is not the same product even where the category matches.

POLICY NOTE PN-2026-1 (effective 1 March 2026). S1.1 is amended so that a like-for-like item may be priced up to 10% higher than the ordered item; the difference is charged to the customer. The requirement of equal or lower price is withdrawn.

CASE

Order date: 18 April 2026
Account setting: allow substitutions: ON
Ordered: Silverbrook almond drink, unsweetened, 1 L, category "plant milks", listed allergens: tree nuts (almond). Price 2.40
Delivered: Oakhaven almond drink, unsweetened, 1 L, category "plant milks", listed allergens: tree nuts (almond). Price 2.60
Shopper's app note: "Silverbrook out of stock, swapped to Oakhaven, same thing."
Approval requested in app: no

Damage or date issue reported: none

question.instructions: Decide whether the customer is entitled to a full refund of the substituted item under SP-3 as amended. Answer yes if a full refund is due, no if not.

criteria.true: The substitution was unapproved and outside the exception, so a full refund is due.
criteria.false: The substitution was permitted without approval and no full refund is due.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-eval-mixed
provenance.rationale: The account allows substitutions, so S1.1 applies. Both items are in the 'plant milks' category with the identical allergen profile (tree nuts), so under S6 the substitute is the same product, differing only by brand. The price is 2.60 against 2.40, an 8.3% increase, which is within the 10% tolerance introduced by PN-2026-1. The substitution was therefore like-for-like and permitted without approval; the customer is charged the 0.20 difference and no full refund is due. S2 is irrelevant.
provenance.why_hard: Under the original S1.1 the higher price alone would have made the swap unauthorised, and no approval was requested.
